q: What is the cell type of plants?
exp: Plant cells are eukaryotic, meaning their basic cellular organisation is of the eukaryotic type. This is one of the broad characteristics used to describe the Plant Kingdom.

q: Which statement best describes cellular organisation in the plant groups covered in this chapter?
a: Most are multicellular, but some algae may be unicellular or colonial.
exp: Most plant groups are multicellular, but algae are variable: Chlamydomonas is unicellular, Volvox is colonial and Spirogyra is filamentous. Therefore 'all plants are multicellular' is too absolute here.

q: Which statement about movement in plants is most accurate?
a: Most land plants are sessile, although some algal cells or gametes may be motile.
exp: The usual land-plant body is sessile, but some algal cells and reproductive stages are motile. The qualified statement avoids an over-generalisation.

q: Which statement best describes nutrition in the Plant Kingdom?
a: Photosynthetic autotrophy is predominant, with some parasitic or partially heterotrophic exceptions.
exp: Most green plants are photosynthetic autotrophs. Parasitic plants and insectivorous plants are important exceptions or supplements to this general pattern.

q: What type of cell wall do plants have?
exp: A cellulosic cell wall is a characteristic plant feature. Cellulose is the material highlighted for the plant cell wall.

q: Which organelles are characteristic of plant cells?
exp: Plastids are highlighted as characteristic organelles of plant cells. They form part of the feature-set that distinguishes plants from animals in this classification.

q: Which set of structures is characteristically associated with plant cells rather than animal cells?
a: Cellulosic cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole.
exp: A cellulosic wall, plastids and a prominent central vacuole are classic plant-cell features. 'Sessile nature' is not a cell structure and is not exclusive to plants.

q: Into which two broad subkingdoms is the Plant Kingdom divided?
exp: The broad division used here separates the Plant Kingdom into Cryptogams and Phanerogams. Cryptogams are seedless, whereas Phanerogams are seed-bearing.

q: Are seeds present in Cryptogams?
exp: Seeds are absent in Cryptogams. They reproduce by spores and have inconspicuous or hidden reproductive organs.

q: Which statement best describes reproduction in Cryptogams in the traditional classification?
a: They do not form seeds and commonly reproduce through spores or other non-seed reproductive stages.
exp: The key exam point is absence of seeds. Bryophytes and pteridophytes form spores, while algae may reproduce vegetatively, asexually by spores and sexually by gametes.

q: How are the reproductive organs of Cryptogams described?
exp: The reproductive organs of Cryptogams are described as inconspicuous or hidden. This contrasts with the external cone or flower associated with Phanerogams.

q: Which main groups are included under Cryptogams?
exp: Cryptogams include Thallophyta, Bryophyta and Pteridophyta. All three are seedless groups, although they differ in body differentiation and vascular tissue.

q: Which statement correctly describes Phanerogams in the traditional classification?
a: They are seed-bearing plants with conspicuous reproductive structures.
exp: Phanerogams are the traditional seed-plant group; their reproductive structures are conspicuous, represented by cones in Gymnosperms and flowers in Angiosperms.

q: How are the reproductive structures of Phanerogams best described in the traditional classification?
a: Conspicuous and well developed—cones in gymnosperms and flowers in angiosperms.
exp: Phanerogams are seed plants with conspicuous reproductive structures: gymnosperms bear strobili/cones and angiosperms bear flowers.

q: Which main groups are included under Phanerogams?
exp: Phanerogams include Gymnosperms and Angiosperms. Both bear seeds, but Gymnosperm seeds are naked while Angiosperm seeds are covered by the ovary or fruit.

q: What does Thallophyta have instead of a differentiated plant body?
exp: Thallophyta has an undifferentiated thallus instead of a body divided into true roots, stems and leaves.

q: What key vascular feature is absent in Bryophyta?
exp: Bryophyta lacks vascular tissue. This is an important contrast with Pteridophyta, where vascular tissue is present.

q: What root-like structures are present in Bryophyta?
exp: Bryophytes possess rhizoids instead of true roots. Rhizoids are therefore an important body feature for identifying Bryophyta.

q: What major body features are present in Pteridophyta?
a: Vascular tissues and true roots, stems and leaves.
exp: Pteridophyta possesses vascular tissues together with true roots, stems and leaves. It is therefore more differentiated than Bryophyta while still remaining seedless.

q: What kind of seeds are found in Gymnosperms?
exp: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds. Their seeds are not enclosed by an ovary or fruit.

q: How are Angiosperm seeds covered?
a: They are enclosed by the ovary / fruit.
exp: Angiosperm seeds are enclosed by the ovary or fruit. This covered-seed condition separates Angiosperms from Gymnosperms.

q: Into which two groups are Angiosperms further divided?
exp: Angiosperms are divided into Monocots and Dicots. The distinction is later compared through cotyledons, roots, vascular bundles, venation and floral whorls.

q: What is the key seed difference between Cryptogams and Phanerogams?
a: Cryptogams = seeds absent; Phanerogams = seeds present.
exp: The key distinction is seed presence: Cryptogams are seedless, while Phanerogams bear seeds.

q: What is the key seed-covering difference between Gymnosperms and Angiosperms?
a: Gymnosperms = naked seeds; Angiosperms = seeds covered by ovary/fruit.
exp: Gymnosperms have naked seeds, whereas Angiosperm seeds are covered by the ovary or fruit. Seed covering is therefore the quickest distinction between these two seed-plant groups.

q: Which set of characters is most useful for comparing the major plant groups?
a: Body organisation, vascular tissue, seed formation and reproductive/life-cycle features.
exp: Major groups are best compared using several characters together, especially body differentiation, vascular tissues, seeds and reproductive/life-cycle traits.

q: Which plant group is clearly gametophyte-dominant in the standard NCERT comparison?
exp: Bryophytes have a dominant independent gametophyte and a dependent sporophyte. Algae do not have one universally dominant generation because their life cycles vary.

q: Which three groups are sporophyte-dominant?
exp: Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms are sporophyte-dominant. This contrasts with Thallophyta and Bryophyta, where the gametophyte is dominant.

q: Which statement correctly describes seed formation in Thallophyta (algae)?
exp: Algae are seedless organisms. In the traditional cryptogam concept they are grouped among plants that do not form seeds.

q: Which statement about vascular tissue in Thallophyta (algae) is correct?
a: True xylem and phloem are absent.
exp: Algae have a thalloid body and lack true vascular tissues such as xylem and phloem.

q: Which statement best describes the plant body of Thallophyta (algae)?
a: It is thalloid and not differentiated into true root, stem and leaves.
exp: The algal plant body is a thallus; true roots, stems and leaves are not differentiated.

q: Which statement about the dominant generation in algae is most accurate?
a: There is no single universal pattern; algal life cycles vary among groups.
exp: Algae show haplontic, diplontic and haplo-diplontic life cycles. Hence 'gametophyte dominant in all algae' is not a safe statement.

q: Give examples of Thallophyta (Algae).
exp: Typical examples are Spirogyra, Chlamydomonas and Sargassum. These examples should be linked with the full Thallophyta profile rather than memorised in isolation.

q: Which reproductive statement is correct for Bryophyta?
a: They are seedless and produce spores.
exp: Bryophytes are seedless plants; the sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.

q: Which statement about vascular tissue in Bryophyta is correct?
a: True xylem and phloem are absent.
exp: Bryophytes are non-vascular plants and lack true xylem and phloem.

q: What is the status of true root, stem and leaf in Bryophyta?
exp: In Bryophyta, true roots, stems and leaves are absent; rhizoids occur. This body feature helps separate it from neighbouring plant groups.

q: Which generation is dominant in Bryophyta?
exp: The dominant generation in Bryophyta is the gametophyte. Bryophyta is seedless and non-vascular, lacks true roots, stems and leaves, bears rhizoids and has a dominant gametophyte.

q: Give examples of Bryophyta.
exp: Typical examples are Marchantia, Funaria and Sphagnum. These examples should be linked with the full Bryophyta profile rather than memorised in isolation.

q: Which reproductive feature correctly describes Pteridophyta?
a: They are seedless vascular plants that reproduce by spores.
exp: Pteridophytes possess vascular tissues but do not form seeds; their sporangia produce spores.

q: Is vascular tissue present in Pteridophyta?
exp: In Pteridophyta, vascular tissue is present. Pteridophyta is seedless but vascular, has true roots, stems and leaves, and has a dominant sporophyte.

q: What is the status of true root, stem and leaf in Pteridophyta?
exp: In Pteridophyta, true roots, stems and leaves are present. This body feature helps separate it from neighbouring plant groups.

q: Which generation is dominant in Pteridophyta?
exp: The dominant generation in Pteridophyta is the sporophyte. Pteridophyta is seedless but vascular, has true roots, stems and leaves, and has a dominant sporophyte.

q: Give examples of Pteridophyta.
exp: Typical examples are ferns, Selaginella, Equisetum and Pteris. These examples should be linked with the full Pteridophyta profile rather than memorised in isolation.

q: Are seeds present in Gymnosperm?
exp: In Gymnosperm, seeds are present and naked. Gymnosperms are vascular seed plants with naked seeds, true roots, stems and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.

q: Is vascular tissue present in Gymnosperm?
exp: In Gymnosperm, vascular tissue is present. Gymnosperms are vascular seed plants with naked seeds, true roots, stems and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.

q: What is the status of true root, stem and leaf in Gymnosperm?
exp: In Gymnosperm, true roots, stems and leaves are present. This body feature helps separate it from neighbouring plant groups.

q: Which generation is dominant in Gymnosperm?
exp: The dominant generation in Gymnosperm is the sporophyte. Gymnosperms are vascular seed plants with naked seeds, true roots, stems and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.

q: Give examples of Gymnosperm.
exp: Typical examples are Cycas, Pinus, Ginkgo and Gnetum. These examples should be linked with the full Gymnosperm profile rather than memorised in isolation.

q: Are seeds present in Angiosperm?
exp: In Angiosperm, seeds are present and covered. Angiosperms are vascular seed plants with covered seeds, true roots, stems and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.

q: Is vascular tissue present in Angiosperm?
exp: In Angiosperm, vascular tissue is present. Angiosperms are vascular seed plants with covered seeds, true roots, stems and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.

q: What is the status of true root, stem and leaf in Angiosperm?
exp: In Angiosperm, true roots, stems and leaves are present. This body feature helps separate it from neighbouring plant groups.

q: Which generation is dominant in Angiosperm?
exp: The dominant generation in Angiosperm is the sporophyte. Angiosperms are vascular seed plants with covered seeds, true roots, stems and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.

q: Give examples of Angiosperm.
exp: Typical examples are Wheat, Rose, Mango and Corn. These examples should be linked with the full Angiosperm profile rather than memorised in isolation.

q: What is the body form of Thallophyta / Algae?
exp: Thallophyta has a thallus-like, undifferentiated body. It is not divided into true roots, stems and leaves.

q: Which statement about vascular tissues in algae is correct?
a: True xylem and phloem are absent.
exp: Algae are thalloid organisms and do not possess true vascular tissues such as xylem and phloem.

q: Which statement best describes tissue differentiation in algae?
a: True vascular and mechanical tissues are not differentiated.
exp: Because the algal body is a thallus, true vascular and mechanical tissue systems are not differentiated as in higher plants.

q: Where are algae mostly found?
exp: Algae are mostly found in aquatic habitats. Their major role as primary producers and contributors to aquatic carbon-dioxide fixation is linked with this habitat.

q: Which statement about life-cycle dominance in algae is correct?
a: It varies among algal groups; no single generation is universally dominant.
exp: Algae exhibit diverse life cycles, so a universal 'gametophyte-dominant' label is incorrect.

q: What are the usual two layers of the rigid cell wall in green algae (Chlorophyceae)?
a: Outer pectose layer and inner cellulose layer.
exp: NCERT describes the usual green-algal wall as an inner cellulose layer and an outer pectose layer. 'Pectose' is the textbook wording.

q: Which substance forms the outer layer of the usual green-algal cell wall?
exp: In Chlorophyceae, the usual rigid wall has an inner cellulose layer and an outer pectose layer.

q: Which layer forms the inner part of the thick green-algal cell wall?
exp: Cellulose forms the inner layer of the thick green-algal cell wall; pectin is the outer layer.

q: What are pyrenoids in green algae?
a: Storage bodies in chloroplasts that contain protein besides starch.
exp: Most green algae have one or more pyrenoids in their chloroplasts. NCERT states that pyrenoids contain protein besides starch, so calling them merely 'starch bodies' is incomplete.

q: Where are Pyrenoids present?
exp: Pyrenoids are present in chloroplasts. They are described as starch bodies in most green algae.

q: What structure helps Laminaria attach to rocks?
exp: Laminaria attaches to rocks by a holdfast. The holdfast anchors the marine alga to the substrate.

q: Laminaria is described as what kind of alga?
exp: Laminaria is a marine alga. It is also one of the examples associated with Phaeophyceae, the brown algae.

q: According to NCERT, approximately how much of Earth's total carbon dioxide fixation is carried out by algae?
exp: NCERT states that at least half of Earth's total carbon dioxide fixation is carried out by algae through photosynthesis.

q: What role do algae play in aquatic food chains?
exp: Algae act as primary producers in aquatic food chains. They form the producer level on which higher trophic levels depend.

q: Which set contains marine algae mentioned by NCERT as being used as food?
exp: NCERT specifically mentions species of Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum among marine algae used as food.

q: Algin is obtained from which type of algae?
exp: Algin is obtained from brown algae. This is a key product-group pair: brown algae → Algin.

q: Carrageenan is obtained from which type of algae?
exp: Carrageenan is obtained from red algae. This forms the contrasting product pair to Algin, which is linked with brown algae.

q: Agar is obtained from which algae?
exp: Agar is obtained from Gelidium and Gracilaria, both associated with red algae in this classification.

q: Gelidium and Gracilaria belong to which colour group of algae?
exp: Gelidium and Gracilaria are red algae. They are also the two algae associated with agar production.

q: Which unicellular alga is specifically mentioned by current NCERT as a protein-rich food supplement used even by space travellers?
exp: Current NCERT specifically mentions Chlorella in this context. Spirulina is a protein-rich cyanobacterium/SCP but is not a true alga in modern classification.

q: What type of products are Algin and Carrageenan?
exp: Algin and Carrageenan are hydrocolloids. Algin is obtained from brown algae, whereas Carrageenan is obtained from red algae.

q: Which algal product is the classic brown-algae trap?
exp: Algin is the product linked with brown algae. Do not confuse it with Carrageenan, which is linked with red algae.

q: Which algal product is the classic red-algae trap?
exp: Carrageenan is the product linked with red algae. Algin, by contrast, is linked with brown algae.

q: Which two red algae are associated with Agar?
exp: Gelidium and Gracilaria are the two red algae associated with agar. This links both their colour group and their commercial product.

q: What is the common description of Chlorophyceae (Green Algae)?
exp: Chlorophyceae is described as green algae. Its pigment, reserve-food and example profile provides the fuller identification.

q: Which pigments occur in Chlorophyceae (Green Algae)?
exp: Chlorophyceae contains chlorophyll-a and b. The pigment combination is one of the quickest ways to distinguish the three major algal classes.

q: What is the stored food in Chlorophyceae (Green Algae)?
exp: The stored food of Chlorophyceae is starch. Reserve food is a key comparison point among green, brown and red algae.

q: Give examples of Chlorophyceae (Green Algae).
exp: Examples of Chlorophyceae are Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Spirogyra. Link these names with the class's colour, pigments and stored food for reliable recall.

q: What is the common description of Phaeophyceae (Brown Algae)?
exp: Phaeophyceae is described as brown algae that are usually marine. Its pigment, reserve-food and example profile provides the fuller identification.

q: Which pigments occur in Phaeophyceae (Brown Algae)?
exp: Phaeophyceae contains chlorophyll-a and c together with fucoxanthin. The pigment combination is one of the quickest ways to distinguish the three major algal classes.

q: What is the stored food in Phaeophyceae (Brown Algae)?
exp: The stored food of Phaeophyceae is mannitol and laminarin. Reserve food is a key comparison point among green, brown and red algae.

q: Give examples of Phaeophyceae (Brown Algae).
exp: Examples of Phaeophyceae are Fucus, Ectocarpus, Sargassum and Laminaria. Link these names with the class's colour, pigments and stored food for reliable recall.

q: What is the common description of Rhodophyceae (Red Algae)?
exp: Rhodophyceae is described as red algae that are usually marine. Its pigment, reserve-food and example profile provides the fuller identification.

q: Which pigments occur in Rhodophyceae (Red Algae)?
exp: Rhodophyceae contains chlorophyll-a and d together with phycoerythrin. The pigment combination is one of the quickest ways to distinguish the three major algal classes.

q: What is the stored food in Rhodophyceae (Red Algae)?
exp: The stored food of Rhodophyceae is Floridean starch. Reserve food is a key comparison point among green, brown and red algae.

q: Give examples of Rhodophyceae (Red Algae).
exp: Examples of Rhodophyceae are Polysiphonia, Porphyra and Gracilaria. Link these names with the class's colour, pigments and stored food for reliable recall.

q: Which pigment is characteristic of brown algae?
exp: Fucoxanthin is the characteristic pigment highlighted for brown algae. Phaeophyceae also contains chlorophyll-a and c.

q: Which pigment is characteristic of red algae?
exp: Phycoerythrin is the characteristic pigment highlighted for red algae. Rhodophyceae also contains chlorophyll-a and d.

q: What is the stored food of green algae?
exp: Green algae store food as starch. This contrasts with mannitol and laminarin in brown algae and Floridean starch in red algae.

q: What are the stored foods of brown algae?
exp: Brown algae store mannitol and laminarin. This food reserve is a useful identifying feature of Phaeophyceae.

q: What is the stored food of red algae?
exp: Red algae store Floridean starch. This distinguishes their reserve food from ordinary starch in green algae and mannitol-laminarin in brown algae.

q: How is Spirogyra described?
exp: Spirogyra is a freshwater filamentous green alga. It is also grouped with Chlorophyceae.

q: Which algal class contains Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Spirogyra?
exp: Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Spirogyra are examples of Chlorophyceae. This class is green, contains chlorophyll-a and b, and stores starch.

q: Which algal class contains Fucus, Ectocarpus, Sargassum and Laminaria?
exp: Fucus, Ectocarpus, Sargassum and Laminaria are examples of Phaeophyceae. This class is brown, usually marine, contains fucoxanthin and stores mannitol and laminarin.

q: Which algal class contains Polysiphonia, Porphyra and Gracilaria?
exp: Polysiphonia, Porphyra and Gracilaria are examples of Rhodophyceae. This class is red, usually marine, contains phycoerythrin and stores Floridean starch.

q: Where are Bryophytes commonly found?
exp: Bryophytes are commonly associated with wet and moist habitats. Although they are land plants, water remains necessary for their reproduction.

q: Which statement best describes roots, stems and leaves in Bryophytes?
a: True roots, stems and leaves are absent; root-like, stem-like or leaf-like structures may occur.
exp: Bryophytes lack true roots, stems and leaves, although structures resembling these organs may occur. Rhizoids attach the plant to the substratum.

q: Which root-like structures occur in Bryophyta?
exp: Rhizoids are the root-like structures of Bryophytes. They are an important clue because Bryophytes lack true roots.

q: Which statement about vascular tissue in Bryophyta is correct?
a: True xylem and phloem are absent.
exp: Bryophytes are non-vascular plants; they do not possess true xylem and phloem.

q: Which generation is dominant in Bryophyta?
exp: The gametophytic generation is dominant in Bryophyta. The sporophyte remains dependent on the gametophyte.

q: On which generation does the Bryophyte sporophyte depend?
exp: The Bryophyte sporophyte depends on the gametophyte. This dependence fits the gametophyte-dominant life cycle of Bryophyta.

q: Why are Bryophytes called “Amphibians of Plant Kingdom”?
a: They are land plants associated with wet/moist conditions and require water for reproduction.
exp: Bryophytes live on land in wet or moist conditions but require water for reproduction. This combination of terrestrial life and reproductive dependence on water gives them the nickname 'Amphibians of Plant Kingdom'.

q: What nickname is given to Bryophyta?
exp: Bryophyta is called the 'Amphibians of Plant Kingdom' because it is terrestrial yet requires water for reproduction.

q: What type of sexual reproduction is noted for Bryophyta?
exp: Bryophyta is described as oogamous. This is the sexual-reproduction type associated with the group.

q: What is the vascular-tissue difference between Bryophyta and Pteridophyta?
a: Bryophyta = vascular tissue absent; Pteridophyta = vascular tissue present.
exp: Bryophyta lacks vascular tissue, whereas Pteridophyta possesses it. This single contrast is one of the fastest ways to separate the two groups.

q: Which statement correctly describes the body of liverworts?
a: Marchantia is thalloid, while some liverworts may have small leaf-like appendages.
exp: NCERT describes Marchantia as thalloid and also notes leafy liverworts with tiny leaf-like appendages. Hence 'all liverworts are thalloid' is too broad.

q: Give examples of liverworts.
exp: Marchantia and Riccia are liverwort examples. They should be separated from moss examples such as Funaria and Sphagnum.

q: Which structures are characteristic of Marchantia?
a: Archegoniophore, Gemma cup, Thallus and Rhizoid.
exp: Marchantia is associated with an archegoniophore, gemma cup, thallus and rhizoid. These structures make the Marchantia identification more specific than merely calling it a liverwort.

q: How is the second stage of the moss gametophyte described?
a: A leafy stage with upright slender axes bearing spirally arranged leaf-like structures.
exp: In mosses, the gametophyte has a protonema stage followed by a leafy stage. Hornworts should not be merged with mosses in this statement.

q: Where are spores produced in mosses / hornworts?
exp: Spores are produced in a capsule. In mosses, those spores can develop into a protonema.

q: What develops from spores in mosses?
exp: A protonema develops from moss spores. It is therefore the stage directly linked with spore germination in mosses.

q: Which set contains only mosses?
exp: NCERT lists Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum as common mosses. Marchantia and Riccia are liverworts.

q: What is Funaria commonly called?
exp: Funaria is called Cord Moss. This name should be distinguished from Sphagnum, which is called Bog Moss or Peat Moss.

q: What is Sphagnum commonly called?
exp: Sphagnum is called Bog Moss. It is also associated with the name Peat Moss.

q: Which additional name and use are associated with Sphagnum?
a: Peat moss; peat has historically been used as fuel.
exp: Sphagnum is also called Peat Moss, and peat has historically been used as fuel. This links the plant name with its use-related fact.

q: Marchantia belongs to which Bryophyte type?
exp: Marchantia is a liverwort. Liverworts are associated with a thalloid body, and Riccia is another example.

q: Funaria belongs to which Bryophyte type?
exp: Funaria is a moss and is also known as Cord Moss. Mosses have a leafy body, produce spores in a capsule and develop a protonema from spores.

q: Sphagnum belongs to which Bryophyte type?
exp: Sphagnum is a moss. It is associated with the names Bog Moss and Peat Moss.

q: Which descriptive term is commonly used for Pteridophytes in traditional exam classification?
exp: Pteridophytes are traditionally called vascular cryptogams because they possess vascular tissues but do not form seeds.

q: What important evolutionary landmark is associated with Pteridophyta?
a: They are the first land plants with vascular tissue.
exp: Pteridophyta is identified as the first land-plant group with vascular tissue. It combines vascular tissue and true roots, stems and leaves with a seedless life cycle.

q: Where are Pteridophytes commonly found?
exp: Pteridophytes are commonly found in damp and shady places. Water is still necessary for their sexual reproduction.

q: Which statement best describes the Pteridophyte sporophyte?
a: It has true roots, stem and leaves with well-differentiated vascular tissues.
exp: The dominant Pteridophyte sporophyte is differentiated into true roots, stem and leaves and contains well-developed vascular tissues.

q: Which vascular tissues are present in Pteridophyta?
exp: Pteridophyta contains xylem and phloem. The presence of these vascular tissues is a defining advance over Bryophyta.

q: Why is water required during sexual reproduction in Pteridophytes?
a: For transfer of motile antherozoids from antheridium to the archegonium.
exp: Water is required for movement of the male gametes (antherozoids) from the antheridium to the archegonium containing the egg.

q: What is the main plant body of Pteridophyta?
exp: The main plant body of Pteridophyta is the sporophyte. The same generation is also the dominant generation.

q: Which generation is dominant in Pteridophyta?
exp: The sporophyte is dominant in Pteridophyta. This contrasts with the gametophyte dominance of Thallophyta and Bryophyta.

q: Where are male gametes formed in Pteridophyta?
exp: Male gametes are formed in the antheridium. This reproductive structure is an important Pteridophyta recall point.

q: Which of the following is the correct set of Pteridophyta examples?
a: Selaginella, Pteris, Equisetum and Psilotum; ferns are also highlighted.
exp: Selaginella, Pteris, Equisetum and Psilotum are Pteridophyta examples, and ferns are also associated with the group.

q: Which group is regarded as the first land plants with vascular tissue?
exp: Pteridophyta is regarded as the first land-plant group with vascular tissue. It is seedless but possesses xylem, phloem and true roots, stems and leaves.

q: Which statement correctly describes Pteridophyte reproduction?
a: Seeds are absent; spores are produced in sporangia.
exp: Pteridophytes are vascular but seedless; their sporangia produce spores by meiosis.

q: Equisetum is placed in which pteridophyte class in NCERT?
exp: NCERT classifies Pteridophytes into Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum) and Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).

q: Which genus is directly associated with the class Sphenopsida in the NCERT classification of Pteridophytes?
exp: The NCERT class–genus association is Sphenopsida → Equisetum. This is more syllabus-safe than an unnecessary 'only living representative' claim.

q: What does “Gymno” mean?
exp: The word part 'Gymno' means naked. In Gymnosperms this refers to the naked condition of the seeds.

q: What does “Sperma” mean?
exp: The word part 'Sperma' means seed. Together, Gymno + Sperma expresses the idea of naked seeds.

q: What type of seeds occur in Gymnosperms?
exp: Gymnosperms have naked seeds because an ovary is absent, so the seeds are not enclosed inside a fruit.

q: Which statement correctly describes the ovules of Gymnosperms?
a: They are not enclosed by an ovary wall and remain exposed.
exp: Gymnosperm ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall; they remain exposed before and after fertilisation, so the resulting seeds are naked.

q: Why do true fruits not form in Gymnosperms?
exp: A true fruit develops from an ovary. Gymnosperms lack an ovary, so their seeds are not enclosed within a true fruit.

q: Which statement about flowers in Gymnosperms is correct?
a: True flowers are absent; reproductive structures occur on sporophylls, often organised into strobili/cones.
exp: Gymnosperms do not bear true flowers. Their microsporangia and ovules are borne on sporophylls, commonly arranged in strobili or cones.

q: Why are fruits absent in Gymnosperms?
exp: Fruits are absent because the ovary is absent. This also leaves the seeds naked rather than enclosed inside a fruit.

q: What is the main plant body in Gymnosperms?
exp: The main plant body of Gymnosperms is the sporophyte. The sporophyte is also the dominant generation in this seed-plant group.

q: Which statement best describes the vegetative body of Gymnosperms?
a: A well-developed sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves.
exp: Gymnosperms have a dominant, well-developed sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves.

q: Which statement about Gymnosperm leaves is most accurate?
a: Leaves may be simple or compound; needle-like leaves are especially characteristic of conifers.
exp: NCERT states that Gymnosperm leaves may be simple or compound. Needle-like leaves are especially a conifer adaptation; Cycas, for example, has pinnate leaves.

q: How are the reproductive structures of Gymnosperms best described?
a: Male and female reproductive structures are borne on sporophylls, often organised into separate strobili/cones.
exp: Gymnosperm microsporophylls and megasporophylls bear the reproductive structures and are commonly arranged in strobili/cones. Cycas is an important exception because its female megasporophylls do not form a compact female cone.

q: In traditional competitive-exam terminology, what is the ploidy of the nutritive tissue commonly called 'endosperm' in Gymnosperms?
a: Haploid (n), because it is the female gametophyte formed before fertilisation.
exp: In many exam books the pre-fertilisation female gametophyte of Gymnosperms is called 'endosperm'; it is haploid. This differs from the typically triploid post-fertilisation endosperm of Angiosperms.

q: Which phloem condition is characteristic of most Gymnosperms?
a: Sieve cells are present, but companion cells are absent.
exp: Gymnosperm phloem generally has sieve cells and lacks the companion cells typical of Angiosperm sieve tubes.

q: Which statement about xylem vessels in Gymnosperms is most accurate?
a: They are generally absent, but occur in Gnetales such as Gnetum.
exp: Most Gymnosperms lack vessels and conduct water mainly through tracheids. Gnetales, including Gnetum, are a standard exception where vessels occur.

q: Which statement best describes the habit of Gymnosperms?
a: They are mostly woody trees or shrubs; many are evergreen, with exceptions.
exp: Gymnosperms are mainly woody trees and shrubs. Many are evergreen, but evergreen habit is not universal, so 'all are evergreen' should be avoided.

q: Give examples of Gymnosperms.
exp: Cycas, Pinus, Ginkgo and Gnetum are Gymnosperm examples. They should be associated with naked seeds and cone-bearing reproduction.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the nutritive tissue commonly called endosperm in Gymnosperms with Angiosperm endosperm?
a: Gymnosperm nutritive female gametophyte is haploid (n); typical Angiosperm endosperm is triploid (3n).
exp: For exam purposes, Gymnosperm 'endosperm' refers to the haploid female gametophyte formed before fertilisation; Angiosperm endosperm usually forms after triple fusion and is triploid.

q: What kind of flowers are present in Angiosperms?
exp: Angiosperms possess well-developed flowers. Flower presence is one of the clear contrasts with Gymnosperms, where true flowers are absent.

q: What type of seeds occur in Angiosperms?
exp: Angiosperms have covered seeds. The seeds are enclosed by the ovary or fruit rather than remaining naked.

q: After fertilisation in Angiosperms, where are the seeds enclosed?
a: Inside the fruit, which develops from the ovary.
exp: In Angiosperms, ovules develop into seeds and the ovary develops into the fruit; therefore the seeds are enclosed within the fruit.

q: Which statement correctly describes fruit formation in Angiosperms?
a: The ovary normally develops into a fruit after fertilisation.
exp: The ovary generally develops into the fruit after fertilisation, while the ovules develop into seeds.

q: Which structure develops into the fruit in Angiosperms?
exp: The ovary develops into the fruit. The fruit then contains seeds derived from ovules.

q: What does the fruit contain?
exp: The fruit contains seeds derived from ovules. This follows the Angiosperm sequence in which the ovary forms the fruit and ovules give rise to seeds.

q: Which special fertilisation process occurs in Angiosperms?
exp: Double fertilisation is a special Angiosperm process. It is linked with triple fusion and the formation of triploid (3n) endosperm.

q: Which fusion process occurs in Angiosperms?
exp: Triple fusion is highlighted in Angiosperms. It is one of the reproductive events paired with double fertilisation and triploid endosperm.

q: What is the ploidy of Angiosperm endosperm?
exp: Angiosperm endosperm is triploid (3n). This contrasts directly with the haploid (n) endosperm of Gymnosperms.

q: Into which two groups are Angiosperms divided?
exp: Angiosperms are divided into Monocots and Dicots. Their comparison uses cotyledon number, root type, vascular-bundle arrangement, venation and floral whorls.

q: Which three reproductive features characterise Angiosperms?
a: Double fertilisation + Triple fusion + Triploid endosperm.
exp: The three linked Angiosperm features are double fertilisation, triple fusion and triploid endosperm. These should be recalled as one reproductive feature-set.

q: What is the endosperm trap for Angiosperms?
exp: Angiosperm endosperm is triploid (3n). Do not confuse it with Gymnosperm endosperm, which is haploid (n).

q: Which statement correctly describes Gymnosperm seeds?
a: They are naked because the ovules are not enclosed by an ovary wall.
exp: Gymnosperm ovules remain exposed because no ovary wall surrounds them; after fertilisation, the resulting seeds remain naked.

q: Which statement correctly describes Angiosperm seeds?
a: They are enclosed within fruits that develop from ovaries.
exp: Angiosperm ovules are enclosed in an ovary; after fertilisation the ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit.

q: Which reproductive structure is absent in Gymnosperms?
exp: Gymnosperms possess reproductive sporophylls and pollen grains but do not produce true flowers with an ovary.

q: Which structure is characteristic of Angiosperms but absent as a true structure in Gymnosperms?
exp: Angiosperms are flowering plants whose ovules develop inside the ovary. Gymnosperms also produce pollen and possess vascular tissue, so those are not unique to Angiosperms.

q: Which fruit-related statement is correct for Gymnosperms?
a: True fruits are absent because an ovary is absent.
exp: Because Gymnosperms lack an ovary, they do not form true fruits; their seeds remain exposed.

q: Which fruit-related statement is correct for Angiosperms?
a: The ovary generally develops into a fruit containing seeds.
exp: In Angiosperms the ovary typically develops into the fruit and the ovules develop into seeds.

q: What is the endosperm feature of Gymnosperms?
exp: Gymnosperm endosperm is haploid (n), whereas Angiosperm endosperm is triploid (3n). This ploidy contrast is a high-value comparison point.

q: What is the endosperm feature of Angiosperms?
exp: Gymnosperm endosperm is haploid (n), whereas Angiosperm endosperm is triploid (3n). This ploidy contrast is a high-value comparison point.

q: Which statement about double fertilisation in Gymnosperms is correct?
a: The characteristic Angiosperm-type double fertilisation is absent.
exp: The characteristic double fertilisation involving syngamy plus triple fusion is an Angiosperm feature, not the standard Gymnosperm condition.

q: Which statement about double fertilisation in Angiosperms is correct?
a: It includes syngamy and triple fusion.
exp: Angiosperm double fertilisation consists of syngamy and triple fusion; triple fusion usually produces the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.

q: Which phloem feature is typical of Gymnosperms?
a: Companion cells are absent; sieve cells are present.
exp: Gymnosperm phloem generally contains sieve cells but lacks companion cells.

q: Which phloem feature is typical of Angiosperms?
a: Sieve-tube elements are associated with companion cells.
exp: A standard Angiosperm phloem feature is the association of sieve-tube elements with companion cells.

q: How are the ovules positioned in Gymnosperms?
a: They are exposed on megasporophylls and are not enclosed by an ovary wall.
exp: Exposed ovules are a core Gymnosperm feature and are more reliable for comparison than leaf shape, which varies among Gymnosperms.

q: How are the ovules positioned in Angiosperms?
a: They are enclosed within an ovary.
exp: Angiosperm ovules are enclosed within an ovary; after fertilisation, ovules become seeds and the ovary usually becomes the fruit.

q: What is the examples feature of Gymnosperms?
exp: Cycas, Pinus and Ginkgo are Gymnosperm examples, whereas Wheat, Rose and Mango are Angiosperm examples.

q: What is the examples feature of Angiosperms?
exp: Cycas, Pinus and Ginkgo are Gymnosperm examples, whereas Wheat, Rose and Mango are Angiosperm examples.

q: Which set contains three Dicot examples?
exp: Rose, Tomato and Mustard are Dicot examples. They belong with the two-cotyledon, tap-root and reticulate-venation pattern.

q: Seeds absent + spore reproduction points to which broad subkingdom?
exp: Cryptogams are seedless and reproduce by spores. Their reproductive organs are described as inconspicuous or hidden, separating them from seed-bearing Phanerogams.

q: Seeds present + cone/flower points to which broad subkingdom?
exp: Phanerogams are seed-bearing plants with external reproductive organs in the form of a cone or flower. Gymnosperms and Angiosperms belong to this broad division.

q: Undifferentiated thallus with no vascular tissue points to which group?
exp: An undifferentiated thallus together with absence of vascular tissue identifies Thallophyta or Algae. True roots, stems and leaves are not present.

q: Gametophyte dominant + root-like rhizoids + no vascular tissue points to which group?
exp: Bryophyta is gametophyte-dominant, lacks vascular tissue and possesses root-like rhizoids instead of true roots. The combination of all three clues identifies Bryophyta.

q: True root/stem/leaves + vascular tissue + no seeds points to which group?
exp: Pteridophyta combines true roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue but remains seedless. That combination separates it from Bryophyta and seed plants.

q: Naked seeds + no ovary/fruit points to which group?
exp: Gymnosperms have naked seeds because the ovary is absent; consequently fruits are also absent. These linked features identify Gymnosperms.

q: Covered seeds + double fertilisation + triploid endosperm points to which group?
exp: Covered seeds, double fertilisation and triploid endosperm are characteristic Angiosperm features. Triple fusion is the other closely linked reproductive event.

q: Outer pectose + inner cellulose cell wall is characteristic of which algal class?
exp: NCERT describes the usual green-algal wall as an inner cellulose layer and an outer pectose layer.

q: Pyrenoids containing protein besides starch are commonly found in the chloroplasts of which group?
exp: Most Chlorophyceae possess one or more pyrenoids in the chloroplast; these storage bodies contain protein besides starch.

q: Holdfast attachment to rocks is specifically illustrated by which marine alga?
exp: Laminaria is the marine alga associated with a holdfast that anchors it to rocks. Laminaria is also a brown-algal example.

q: Algin points to which algae?
exp: Algin is obtained from brown algae. The paired contrast is Carrageenan from red algae.

q: Carrageenan points to which algae?
exp: Carrageenan is obtained from red algae. Algin is the corresponding product linked with brown algae.

q: Gelidium + Gracilaria point to which product?
exp: Gelidium and Gracilaria are the red algae associated with agar production. Therefore the organism pair directly points to Agar.

q: Which alga is specifically noted in current NCERT as a protein-rich food supplement used even by space travellers?
exp: Current NCERT specifically names Chlorella in this context. Spirulina is a protein-rich cyanobacterium/SCP, not a true alga in modern classification.

q: Fucoxanthin points to which algal class?
exp: Fucoxanthin is the characteristic pigment of Phaeophyceae or brown algae. This class also contains chlorophyll-a and c.

q: Phycoerythrin points to which algal class?
exp: Phycoerythrin is the characteristic pigment of Rhodophyceae or red algae. This class also contains chlorophyll-a and d.

q: Mannitol + Laminarin point to which algae?
exp: Mannitol and Laminarin are the stored foods of brown algae. Their presence is a strong identifying feature of Phaeophyceae.

q: Floridean starch points to which algae?
exp: Floridean starch is the stored food of red algae. It distinguishes Rhodophyceae from green algae storing starch and brown algae storing mannitol-laminarin.

q: Freshwater filamentous green alga points to which example?
exp: Spirogyra is described as a freshwater filamentous green alga. It belongs to Chlorophyceae.

q: “Amphibians of Plant Kingdom” points to which group?
exp: Bryophyta is called the Amphibians of Plant Kingdom because it lives on land in moist conditions but requires water for reproduction.

q: Marchantia + Riccia point to which Bryophyte type?
exp: Marchantia and Riccia are liverworts. Liverworts are associated with a thalloid body.

q: Funaria = which named moss?
exp: Funaria is called Cord Moss. Sphagnum, in contrast, is associated with Bog Moss or Peat Moss.

q: Sphagnum = which named moss?
exp: Sphagnum is called Bog Moss and is also associated with the name Peat Moss. Peat has historically been used as fuel.

q: First land plants with vascular tissue points to which group?
exp: Pteridophyta is regarded as the first land-plant group with vascular tissue. It has true roots, stems and leaves but remains seedless.

q: Male gametes formed in Antheridium points here to which group?
exp: In Pteridophyta, male gametes are formed in the antheridium. This reproductive clue identifies the group in the reverse question.

q: Equisetum is associated with which pteridophyte class in NCERT?
exp: The NCERT association is Sphenopsida → Equisetum.

q: Unisexual cone + naked seed points to which group?
exp: Gymnosperms possess unisexual cones and naked seeds. True flowers and fruits are absent because an ovary is absent.

q: Which statement correctly describes the Gymnosperm nutritive tissue often called endosperm in exam books?
a: It is the haploid (n) female gametophyte formed before fertilisation.
exp: The traditional Gymnosperm 'endosperm' is the haploid female gametophyte and is present before fertilisation.

q: Triploid endosperm points to which seed-plant group?
exp: Triploid (3n) endosperm identifies Angiosperms. It is linked with double fertilisation and triple fusion.

q: Double fertilisation + triple fusion point to which group?
exp: Double fertilisation and triple fusion are characteristic Angiosperm reproductive events. They are also associated with triploid endosperm.

q: One cotyledon + fibrous root + parallel venation points to which group?
exp: One cotyledon, fibrous roots and parallel venation form the classic Monocot pattern. Monocot floral whorls also occur in multiples of 3.

q: Two cotyledons + tap root + reticulate venation points to which group?
exp: Two cotyledons, a tap root and reticulate venation form the classic Dicot pattern. Dicot floral whorls occur in multiples of 4 or 5.

q: Floral whorls in multiples of 3 point to which group?
exp: Floral whorls in multiples of 3 are characteristic of Monocots. This matches their one cotyledon, fibrous roots and parallel venation.

q: Floral whorls in multiples of 4 or 5 point to which group?
exp: Floral whorls in multiples of 4 or 5 are characteristic of Dicots. This matches their two cotyledons, tap roots and reticulate venation.

q: Scattered stem vascular bundles point to which group?
exp: Scattered vascular bundles in the stem are characteristic of Monocots. Dicots instead have vascular bundles arranged in a ring.

q: Stem vascular bundles arranged in a ring point to which group?
exp: Stem vascular bundles arranged in a ring are characteristic of Dicots. Monocots have scattered vascular bundles.

q: Corn, Wheat and Bajra point to which angiosperm class?
exp: Corn, Wheat and Bajra are Monocots. They belong with the one-cotyledon, fibrous-root and parallel-venation pattern.

q: Rose, Chickpea and Tomato point to which angiosperm class?
exp: Rose, Chickpea and Tomato are Dicots. They belong with the two-cotyledon, tap-root and reticulate-venation pattern.

q: What is the cell type of plants?
exp: Plant cells are eukaryotic, meaning their basic cellular organisation is of the eukaryotic type. This is one of the broad characteristics used to describe the Plant Kingdom.

q: What is the main material of the plant cell wall?
exp: Cellulose is the highlighted material of the plant cell wall. A cellulosic wall is one of the characteristic features used to describe plants.

q: Which broad subkingdom has no seeds?
exp: Cryptogams are seedless plants that reproduce by spores. Their reproductive organs are inconspicuous or hidden.

q: Which broad subkingdom has seeds?
exp: Phanerogams are seed-bearing plants. Their reproductive organs occur externally as cones or flowers.

q: What type of body occurs in Thallophyta?
exp: Thallophyta has an undifferentiated thallus instead of a body divided into true roots, stems and leaves.

q: What are the usual cell-wall layers of green algae according to NCERT?
exp: NCERT describes the usual Chlorophyceae wall as an outer pectose layer and an inner cellulose layer.

q: What are pyrenoids in most green algae?
a: Chloroplast storage bodies containing protein besides starch.
exp: Pyrenoids lie in the chloroplasts of most green algae and contain protein besides starch.

q: Which structure attaches Laminaria to rocks?
exp: Laminaria attaches to rocks by a holdfast. The holdfast anchors the marine alga to the substrate.

q: Algin is obtained from which algae?
exp: Algin is obtained from brown algae. The paired contrast is Carrageenan from red algae.

q: Carrageenan is obtained from which algae?
exp: Carrageenan is obtained from red algae. Algin is the corresponding product linked with brown algae.

q: Agar is obtained from which algae?
exp: Agar is obtained from Gelidium and Gracilaria, both associated with red algae in this classification.

q: Which unicellular alga is specifically mentioned by current NCERT as a protein-rich food supplement used by space travellers?
exp: Current NCERT specifically mentions Chlorella as a protein-rich food supplement used even by space travellers.

q: Which pigment is characteristic of brown algae?
exp: Fucoxanthin is the characteristic pigment highlighted for brown algae. Phaeophyceae also contains chlorophyll-a and c.

q: Which pigment is characteristic of red algae?
exp: Phycoerythrin is the characteristic pigment highlighted for red algae. Rhodophyceae also contains chlorophyll-a and d.

q: What is the stored food of green algae?
exp: Green algae store food as starch. This contrasts with mannitol and laminarin in brown algae and Floridean starch in red algae.

q: What is the stored food of brown algae?
exp: Brown algae store mannitol and laminarin. This food reserve is a useful identifying feature of Phaeophyceae.

q: What is the stored food of red algae?
exp: Red algae store Floridean starch. This distinguishes their reserve food from ordinary starch in green algae and mannitol-laminarin in brown algae.

q: How is Spirogyra best described?
exp: Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga commonly found in freshwater habitats.

q: Which group is called the Amphibians of Plant Kingdom?
exp: Bryophyta is called the Amphibians of Plant Kingdom because it lives on land in moist conditions but requires water for reproduction.

q: Which generation is dominant in Bryophyta?
exp: The gametophytic generation is dominant in Bryophyta. The sporophyte remains dependent on the gametophyte.

q: What type of sexual reproduction occurs in Bryophyta?
exp: Bryophyta is described as oogamous. This is the sexual-reproduction type associated with the group.

q: Which pair is an example of liverworts?
exp: Marchantia and Riccia are liverwort examples. They should be separated from moss examples such as Funaria and Sphagnum.

q: What is Funaria commonly called?
exp: Funaria is called Cord Moss. This name should be distinguished from Sphagnum, which is called Bog Moss or Peat Moss.

q: What is Sphagnum commonly called?
exp: Sphagnum is called Bog Moss. It is also associated with the name Peat Moss.

q: Which group is regarded as the first land plants with vascular tissue?
exp: Pteridophyta is regarded as the first land-plant group with vascular tissue. It is seedless but possesses xylem, phloem and true roots, stems and leaves.

q: Which generation is dominant in Pteridophyta?
exp: The sporophyte is dominant in Pteridophyta. This contrasts with the gametophyte dominance of Thallophyta and Bryophyta.

q: Where are male gametes formed in Pteridophyta?
exp: Male gametes are formed in the antheridium. This reproductive structure is an important Pteridophyta recall point.

q: Equisetum belongs to which pteridophyte class?
exp: NCERT places Equisetum under Sphenopsida.

q: What type of seeds occur in Gymnosperms?
exp: Gymnosperms have naked seeds because an ovary is absent, so the seeds are not enclosed inside a fruit.

q: In traditional exam terminology, what is the ploidy of the Gymnosperm nutritive female gametophyte often called endosperm?
exp: The Gymnosperm nutritive female gametophyte is haploid and forms before fertilisation; this is the tissue often called 'endosperm' in traditional exam books.

q: How are Gymnosperm reproductive structures generally organised?
a: On sporophylls, commonly forming male and female strobili/cones.
exp: Gymnosperm microsporangia and ovules occur on sporophylls that are commonly arranged into male and female strobili or cones; Cycas shows an important exception in the organisation of female megasporophylls.

q: What is the ploidy of Angiosperm endosperm?
exp: Angiosperm endosperm is triploid (3n). This contrasts directly with the haploid (n) endosperm of Gymnosperms.

q: Which special fertilisation events occur in Angiosperms?
exp: Double fertilisation and triple fusion are the special reproductive events of Angiosperms. They are linked with triploid (3n) endosperm.

q: How many cotyledons are present in Monocots?
exp: Monocots have one cotyledon. Monocots have one cotyledon, adventitious/fibrous roots, scattered stem vascular bundles, isobilateral leaves with parallel venation, and floral whorls in multiples of 3.

q: How many cotyledons are present in Dicots?
exp: Dicots have two cotyledons. Dicots have two cotyledons, tap roots, stem vascular bundles arranged in a ring, dorsiventral leaves with reticulate venation, and floral whorls in multiples of 4 or 5.

q: Which root system and venation are typical of Monocots?
exp: Monocots characteristically have fibrous roots and parallel venation. These features accompany one cotyledon and floral whorls in multiples of 3.

q: Which root system and venation are typical of Dicots?
exp: Dicots characteristically have a tap-root system and reticulate venation. These features accompany two cotyledons and floral whorls in multiples of 4 or 5.

q: In what multiples do Monocot floral whorls occur?
exp: Monocot floral whorls occur in multiples of 3. This is part of the one-cotyledon, fibrous-root and parallel-venation pattern.

q: In what multiples do Dicot floral whorls occur?
exp: Dicot floral whorls occur in multiples of 4 or 5. This is part of the two-cotyledon, tap-root and reticulate-venation pattern.
